prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The monocular depth map captures an indoor room with a wooden floor sloping away from the camera wearer, a counter or cabinet edge on the right within arm's reach (roughly 0.5–1.0 m away), two floor bowls on a mat about 1.2–1.5 m below and to the right, and distant background furniture and doorways 2.5–4.0 m ahead. Across the five frames, a white-and-brown dog below and in front of the wearer approaches from roughly 1.2 m in frame 1 to about 0.4–0.6 m in frames 3–5 as the wearer crouches or bends closer, while the dog's head tilts upward to look directly toward the camera wearer and comes within arm's reach of the wearer's extended left hand at the bottom center of frames 3–5. The depth map clearly reveals the continuous 3D elevation of the dog's body above the floor, the vertical side of the right cabinet, and the shallow recess of the dog bowls even where shadows and specular floor glare obscure surfaces in the RGB strip. However, the map is unreliable where the wearer's hand and the dog's chin merge into a single saturated white blob in frames 3–5, and where distant legs and chairs in the upper background (2.5–3.5 m away) flatten into the dark background.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates the foreground animal in the lower half of the scene against an unlabelled black background, tracking it as it moves closer from about 1.2 m to 0.5 m in front of and below the camera wearer while turning its head from facing right toward the floor bowls (roughly 0.3–0.5 m to its right) in frames 1–2 to looking up at the wearer in frames 3–5. Although the silhouette captures the dog's overall footprint and shows how its lower legs and tail are partly occluded by its torso or cut off by the frame edges, it fails to segment the nearby counter on the right (0.5–1.0 m), the bowls on the floor (1.2–1.5 m), the distant person's legs near the top (about 2.5–3.0 m away), and the camera wearer's own hand touching the dog's chin within arm's reach (0.4 m) in frames 3–5. In frame 5, the map detects a partial object at the upper left edge (roughly 2.0–2.5 m away, where stacked chairs sit in the RGB) that is easy to overlook in the cluttered background, though it mislabels those chair parts as a person. The map is highly unreliable in its class labels and instance boundaries: it misclassifies the dog as a bird in frame 3 (and a tiny leg fragment as a second bird), overlaps a tiny 'bird' mask on the tail tip in frame 4, and splits the single dog into two separate 'dog' instances (head vs. body) in frame 5 while merging the wearer's hand into the animal mask in frames 3–5.
descriptions.pose: The body and hand skeleton map is completely blank (solid black) across all five frames, providing no spatial skeletons despite the presence of human body parts in the RGB strip. In the RGB context, the camera wearer's own left hand enters from the bottom edge within arm's reach (roughly 0.3–0.5 m from the camera) in frames 3–5 to touch the underside of the dog's chin, while the lower legs and feet of a second person are visible in the upper background (about 2.5–3.5 m away to the upper left in frame 1 and upper center in frame 5, facing away or sideways). Because all human body parts are heavily truncated by the camera frustum—with the camera wearer's body behind the lens and the distant person cut off above the ankles—and the wearer's fingers are partly occluded under the dog's snout, the pose detector fails completely. Consequently, this map reveals nothing that is hard to see in the RGB image and is entirely unreliable for tracking either the wearer's reaching hand movement across frames 3–5 or the distant person's position in the room.
